request.prompt:
The abbey precinct and the headland of the abandoned saltworks at Greyhithe, seen from the south and slightly above, the sea behind.

In front, the cloister: a square garth open to the sky with a covered arcaded walk along its north side, the arcade the same tall narrow round-headed rhythm as the works. A small square chapter house beyond the walk, its one high window lit from inside by a low fire.

Behind them the abbey church, the tallest building here: a long stone box running away from the eye, clerestory windows in the same rhythm, the roof gone over the east end so the sky shows through the ribs.

Beyond the precinct wall the ground falls away and a bare path runs out along a narrow headland with sea on both sides, no cover anywhere on it.

At the far end, a walled square court, and standing in it a squat round stone light tower with a warm lamp burning at the top. Nobody is anywhere in the picture.
request.style_note: The Saltworks at Greyhithe, in one hand throughout: a cold North Sea dusk, the sky a narrow band of pale light low in the west and dark above. One masonry everywhere — grey lias limestone laid in long thin courses, iron-stained red-brown where the sea reaches it, quoins and jambs in the same stone dressed square. One way of letting light in — tall narrow round-headed openings in a repeated rhythm, high in the wall, in the works and in the abbey alike. Slate roofs weathered near-black, salt-bleached timber, no render, no whitewash. One warm lamp burning on the headland, the only warm colour in the picture. Matte gouache on toned grey paper, restrained palette, visible dry brush, no figures, no text, no lettering. Each image is ONE single full-frame view of that place, filling the frame edge to edge: never a sheet, never a grid, never a panel, never an inset or a caption.
